articles.title_orig: European Central Bank keeps key interest rate on hold at 2.5%
articles.title_zh: European Central Bank keeps key interest rate on hold at 2.5%
articles.content_orig:
The European Central Bank voted to hold interest rates steady on Thursday, meeting market expectations, despite euro zone inflation rising to a three-year high.
It keeps the central bank's key rate, the deposit facility, at 2.5% following a 25 basis point hike in September .
In a statement, the institution's Governing Council said rising energy prices posed upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to growth, but that underlying inflation and wages were so far broadly stable.
"At this point in time we are not seeing second round effects in addition to what is already included in the projections" released in September, ECB President Christine Lagarde told CNBC's Annette Weisbach during a press conference.
Lagarde identified the main developments since the ECB's last meeting as higher energy costs across oil, petrol, fuel, gas and refining margins, and a sharp rise in long-term financing costs, with the average 10-year sovereign yield up by around 35 basis points.
"If you combine these two factors — actually, the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate — but on the basis of the uncertainty that accumulates and that rises as well, on the basis of underlying inflation that has broadly remained unchanged, the Governing Council unanimously decided that we were well positioned enough at this stage to hold and that a measured approach at this point in time remained appropriate," Lagarde said.
Money markets were pricing in around a 67% probability of a rate hike in December following the announcement, according to LSEG data.
Headline inflation in the euro area hit 3.8% last month , the highest level since September 2023. Energy price inflation reached 18.8% amid continued turbulence in the Middle East.
The resurgence in energy price pressures following the outbreak of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran in February saw the ECB hike rates in June for the first time since 2023.
The euro area economy continued to expand in the third quarter of the year, with a recovery in services since the start of the Middle East conflict, the Governing Council said in an explanation of its decision Thursday.
Manufacturing, digital services and exports are being boosted by AI-related investments, while government spending on infrastructure and defense is supporting business activity. However, energy price pressures are likely to hit consumer confidence as higher financing costs weigh on growth.
In her press conference, Lagarde said the ECB would continue monitoring rising French borrowing costs and increased fragmentation that has spooked some market watchers.
Lagarde noted borrowing costs at the long end of the curve were rising significantly around the world, which she attributed to expectations for inflation and interest rates as well as "debt issuance by some of the hyperscalers," which she said were issuing more long-term bonds and driving up competition.
"Predicting the path of ECB monetary policy is becoming more challenging," Deutsche Bank's chief European economist, Mark Wall, said in a note on Thursday.
"One question is whether the two hikes already delivered and the tightening of financial conditions since September are enough to lean against the further increase in energy inflation risk? Probably not."
Wall said the other main question was whether the looming departure of Lagarde as ECB president — a decision she announced earlier on Thursday — would impact decision-making next year.
"We think the institution is bigger than the person, but there's uncertainty. We expect one more hike to 2.75% in December while Lagarde is still President, and that's probably the end of the hiking cycle."
Dean Turner, chief euro zone and U.K. economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, said the Thursday decision "should be viewed as a hawkish pause rather than the end of the tightening cycle."
France's fiscal challenge is not expected to change the direction of monetary policy "in the absence of broader financial stress," he said in emailed comments.
"The ECB's focus remains firmly on ensuring that today's energy-driven inflation does not develop into a more persistent problem."

articles.title_orig: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
articles.title_zh: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
articles.content_orig:
A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen.
The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024.
While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering.
Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party.
Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing.
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign.
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption."
In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder".
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively.
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year.
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty.
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest.
Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violating [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption.
The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own".
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote.
Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman.
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members.
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22.
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged.
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment."
Analysts believe one reason for the increased empahsis on discipline – which many interpret as loyalty – is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader.
A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder Communist China.
Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says.
"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look".
Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country.
"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says.
"However, further down the road, such concentration of power may pave the way for a more serious power vacuum when Xi ages and slows down."

articles.title_orig: US couple's retirement dream in ruins after residential cruise scrapped in Cambodia
articles.title_zh: US couple's retirement dream in ruins after residential cruise scrapped in Cambodia
articles.content_orig:
More than 200 passengers, mostly Americans, are stranded in Cambodia after the operator of a luxury U.S. cruise ship that was on a continuous around-the-world voyage ran out of money due to skyrocketing fuel costs .
Villa Vie Residences, the Florida-based operator of the MV Odyssey, said the war with Iran quadrupled fuel costs and forced it to suspend operations on Tuesday.
CEO Mikael Petterson told CBS News in a phone interview Wednesday that Villa Vie Residences was paying an average of $700 a ton for fuel before the war broke out in late February. Since then, it has been paying anywhere from $2,000 to $3,000 per ton.
The Odyssey uses between 700 and 800 tons per month in fuel, Petterson disclosed.
"When you divide it over 300 people on board, it's just backbreaking," Petterson told CBS News. "And this has been going on for nine months. We've tried to do everything we can do."
In a statement, Villa Vie Residences said the per cabin fuel costs rose from an average of $1,800 per month before the war to between $6,000 and $8,000.
The company was unwilling to pass those rising costs on to its passengers, Petterson said.
The Odyssey launched in October 2024 for a continuous around-the-world journey. At the time, passengers could become residents of the ship by purchasing a permanent cabin for several hundred thousand dollars. Some sold their homes to do so. At the time, they were given a 15-year minimum guarantee of residency aboard the Odyssey.
The Odyssey attempted to counter the spiking fuel prices by slowing down its itinerary and spending five or six days in each port "hoping that things would come to a close in the Middle East," Petterson said, but it wasn't enough.
"For us, when our monthly expenses go up from $400,000 to $2 million, where are we going to get the $1.6 million?" Petterson asked.
The Villa Vie Residences CEO said that the ship ran out of money as it searched for a financial partner, and the plan is now to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
"We've borrowed money, we've stretched our payrolls as far as we can, and we're at a point where it's just at a breaking point where we need capitalization," Petterson said.
Passenger Benjamin Schatz thought the MV Odyssey would be his forever home.
"Honestly, right now, I'm in denial and in shock, and I'm heartbroken," Schatz, a retiree, told CBS News.
CBS News met Schatz in April 2025 for a story featuring Villa Vie Residences. At that point, he had been living on the ship for about one year. On Wednesday, he was given just hours to pack up his life and leave.
Said Schatz: "There are people now who are homeless and who have very little money and don't know what they're going to do."

articles.title_orig: Decommissioned NVIDIA supercomputer with 9,600 A100 GPUs hits eBay for $60 million, free shipping included
articles.title_zh: Decommissioned NVIDIA supercomputer with 9,600 A100 GPUs hits eBay for $60 million, free shipping included
articles.content_orig:
An IT hardware reseller has listed a decommissioned NVIDIA AI supercomputer on eBay for $59.7 million, or best offer. The seller, Core 4 Solutions, is offering 300 server racks containing 9,600 NVIDIA A100 accelerators and 4,200 AMD EPYC processors. And yes, the listing includes free FedEx Ground shipping. Buyers in a hurry can even select overnight delivery for just $50.
The hardware comes from a decommissioned hyperscaler environment and uses NVIDIA A100 40GB SXM4 accelerators based on the Ampere architecture introduced in 2020. Each rack contains four compute nodes with eight GPUs each, alongside management systems and networking equipment. The complete configuration includes 268,800 Zen 2 CPU cores, 384TB of GPU memory and approximately 1.4PB of combined system memory.
At $59.7 million, the asking price is equivalent to nearly 29,865 GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards at NVIDIA’s official $1,999 MSRP . Or closer to 7500 units at current prices. Of course, this comparison is purely financial, since the A100 is a data center accelerator rather than a gaming GPU. The asking price works out to approximately $6,219 per A100, although that also covers the processors, memory, networking hardware and server racks. The seller also offers individual 32-GPU racks for $199,000.
The bulk listing has since ended with the item marked as no longer available, although there is no confirmation that a sale took place.

articles.title_orig: Serious pollution by water industry remains high despite £5bn investment, say regulators
articles.title_zh: Serious pollution by water industry remains high despite £5bn investment, say regulators
articles.content_orig:
The environmental performance of water companies worsened again last year despite industry investment, according to the first joint report by the regulators.
Eight of the nine companies in England were rated as "poor" or "requiring improvement", with only Severn Trent receiving the highest rating.
Companies were praised for reducing service disruptions but serious pollution into the environment remained a "major concern".
The chair of the environmental regulator, Alan Lovell, said the results showed the industry continued to "fall well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public".
"I'm very angry," he told BBC News. "I think it's extremely disappointing to see the level of pollution incidents... and I completely sympathise with the public."
Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said she was "demanding answers from the companies that are failing" and would be "shining a spotlight on the worst offences around the country".
Four different regulators currently oversee water companies in England and Wales - the Environment Agency (EA), Natural Resources Wales (NRW), Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate - and this marks the first time they have come together to assess the industry.
It is a nod to the commitment made by Sir Keir Starmer's government to merge the organisations covering England into a single body as part of efforts to streamline regulation .
But it is on environmental performance that the report is most critical.
Serious pollution incidents in 2025 were a "major concern", the Environment Agency said, and remained at similarly high levels to those seen in previous years.
Overall, England's water companies were awarded 16 out of a possible 36 stars for environmental performance - the worst total on record.
The EA said this was due to "declining performance in some areas but also due to our tighter performance standards".
And in Wales, Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water was given a two-star rating, out of four, by NRW.
Industry body Water UK acknowledged that "the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough".
But it also pointed out that more than half of all pollution incidents were as a result of "blockages or vandalism, which are not in the direct control of the water companies".
"It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth, and end sewage entering rivers and seas," a spokesperson said.
Today's report did highlight some "strengths to build on", with UK drinking water quality remaining "among the best in the world".
And the regulators also noted that "leakage has reduced over the long term" but said improvement was still needed.
Water companies have committed record levels of investment up to 2030 to upgrade their networks and sewage treatment works. But customer bills are expected to rise 36% on average between 2025 and 2030 as a result.
There has already been £5bn invested over the last five years to try and tackle environmental pollution.
But Alan Lovell from the EA said: "Not all companies have delivered the environmental improvement schemes they have been funded for."
In September, it was reported that the number of complaints made by households about water companies to the Consumer Council for Water (CCW) rose by 84% in a year - the highest in 20 years.
Mike Keil, chief executive of the CCW, said that "many customers have not noticed any improvement in customer service or performance" despite recent bill rises.
"People support investment and understand it takes time to bear fruit," he said, but added that "bill payers are already questioning whether their money is being well spent".
The government is planning to introduce new legislation next year to overhaul the structure and regulation of the industry - including combining the regulators in England.
The Welsh government plans to set up a new regulator alongside Natural Resources Wales.
In his Labour conference speech last month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that a strengthened Water Bill would also remove limits on government ownership of shares in England's major water companies.
He also promised new powers for local leaders . The BBC understands further details on the idea of "regional bodies" to oversee water companies are likely to follow in the coming weeks.
The joint report, published on Thursday, also found that household consumption in England and Wales in 2025 remained similar to the previous year, at 137 litres per person per day.
Government advisers have said that demand for water will likely have to fall to safeguard future supplies , which are facing pressures from climate change, a growing population and historic underinvestment.
Hosepipe bans remain in place across large parts of England and Wales as companies have sought to shore up supplies following drought this summer.
Mark Owen, head of fisheries at the Angling Trust, said the industry also needed to take more responsibility and cut leakage rates further.
"Every litre lost has already been taken from the environment while our rivers, fish and wildlife are under immense pressure," he said.

articles.title_orig: Rate decision live: Interest rates held steady in split vote, Warsh says politics played 'no role' ahead of midterm elections
articles.title_zh: Rate decision live: Interest rates held steady in split vote, Warsh says politics played 'no role' ahead of midterm elections
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Federal Reserve officials voted 10-2 to keep interest rates unchanged, as elevated inflation continues to pose a problem for central bankers. Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-point rate hike.
The Fed's benchmark rates remained in the 3.75% to 4% range , as widely expected. A rate hike in December, however, appears far more likely, according to the Fed's dot plot and fed funds futures.
Here are the key takeaways from the Fed's statement and Fed Chairman Warsh's press conference:
Fed upgrades economy from "solid" to "strong": The FOMC updated the language in its statement, adding that "the accumulation of more information will help" it decide the right policy stance. This suggests the Fed is not in a hurry to ease inflation.
But "inflation remains elevated": Warsh reiterated the Fed's commitment to bringing inflation down to the 2% target. Although recent inflation data came in hotter than expected , the Fed has positioned itself to continue assessing data.
Warsh announces changes to the Fed's schedule : In 2027, one of the eight Fed meetings will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy with neither a vote on the Fed's funds rate nor a policy statement. In 2028, policymakers will hold two meetings dedicated to strategy and six for setting policy.
Warsh refutes the idea that the decision was politically inflected: Warsh stated that "politics played no role in the decision" — something that generated some discussion with the US midterm elections next week.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said he doesn't agree that Fed rate hikes will have no impact on artificial intelligence, given the strong demand for AI and the high returns investors expect.
"I was skeptical of that view," Warsh said during a press conference. "Interest rates get in the cracks. Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything."
Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman, in a post last month on X , expressed skepticism that higher rates would reduce demand and investment in AI.
"What if higher rates don't reduce demand and investment because the demand for intelligence and energy is unaffected by higher rates because winning the race for super intelligence has a near infinite ROI and the demand for compute will remain incalculable," Ackman wrote. "What if the old models don't apply to the current paradigm?"
Warsh pointed to how credit spreads for certain assets have widened since the Fed raised rates in September, and financial conditions have tightened as investors have differentiated between tech firms and other companies to invest.
"With respect to the new technology and this investment surge, do interest rates matter? I believe they do," said Warsh. "And I don't believe that they're somehow divorced from the rest of the economy."
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh pushed back Wednesday on any suggestion that next week's midterm elections had a role in the Fed's decision to keep interest rates steady . He also dodged multiple questions on political topics and pressure coming his way from the Oval Office.
But it wasn't for a lack of trying from the assembled reporters.
"I appreciate the question, but I'm not going to be responding to quotes from public officials," Warsh said during a press conference when presented with criticisms from President Trump that interest rates should be lower and that his colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee were "political."
When the subject turned to the midterm elections, Warsh was similarly curt.
"Politics played no role in the decision," the chair said, adding, "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."
Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes:
The Warsh Fed's taciturn nature has already raised the stakes for each FOMC meeting. With fewer hints or forward guidance about what the Fed is thinking and planning comes more suspense.
And next year, those stakes will be even higher as the Fed removes a rate decision from its calendar, making each meeting even more important and potentially adding another layer of uncertainty and volatility to markets .
At the October policy meeting on Wednesday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced this major change to the Fed's calendar and added that 2028 might feature only six rate decisions. The meetings themselves will remain on the calendar, but instead of the Fed debating rates, broader monetary policy topics will be on the agenda.
Warsh said the reasoning behind the schedule change is to "reserve the time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons."
We've all been wondering how the newly installed chair would reshape the Fed. Already, he's been doing that by changing the nature of the Fed's public communication.
Wall Street can't make up its mind about the Fed.
Stocks dipped after the 2 p.m. statement, rallied as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke, then gave much of that back. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) is holding a small gain, and chip stocks are doing most of the lifting.
The typical stock isn't doing as well. The equal-weighted S&P 500, which gives every company the same weight, is in the red. So are small caps.
The bond market is clearer about what it thinks. The 30-year Treasury yield is near its high of the day, and the 10-year yield is back above 5%. Higher long-term rates make borrowing more expensive for companies and homebuyers.
The dollar moved the other way and slipped against the euro during the press conference.
That leaves the streak. The S&P 500 came into Wednesday down on six straight Fed days, the second-longest run since 1994, which we pointed out at 2:43 p.m. ET. A higher close would end it, and a lower one would tie the 2018 record of seven.
Chairman Warsh said a couple of words on the Fed's independence amid some discussion that the US midterm elections — just six days away — and the perception that the Fed could influence them could sway the Fed's decision.
"Politics played no role in the decision," Warsh stated. "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."
"But I will say," Warsh added, "it's an information-rich interval in the coming period, having nothing to do with politics."
The Fed won't be sitting on its hands for long, says the market.
Traders see about an 85% chance that the Fed raises its benchmark rate by a quarter point at its next meeting on Dec. 9, according to Bloomberg data. The data comes from futures contracts that let traders bet on where the Fed sets rates. Those odds are about where they stood Tuesday, before the decision.
Further out, traders expect the Fed's rate to climb from about 3.9% now to nearly 4.7% by September 2027. That's about three more quarter-point hikes, slightly more than they expected Tuesday.
The Dec. 9 meeting is next. A hike would match what traders already expect. Another hold would mean they've gotten ahead of the Fed.
Chairman Warsh noted that while the Fed waits to assess more inflation data, some policymakers view the central bank's moves so far as beginning to take effect.
"If you were listening next to me in that room the last couple of days, the overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgment, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine starting to work some, but there's no firm conclusions," Warsh said.
"If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today," he added. "What we decided to do was to call these questions, take stock of where we are, evaluate what we're seeing out the window, ask ourselves whether the period right in front of us is likely to provide more clarity on the appropriate protocol."

articles.title_orig: Popular airline hits customers with steep fee hike for first time in 8 years
articles.title_zh: Popular airline hits customers with steep fee hike for first time in 8 years
articles.content_orig:
American Airlines is raising the annual fee for two of its rewards credit cards for the first time since 2018 and adding new benefits like a TSA PreCheck credit and points from spending on hotels.
The fee on the Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select World Elite Mastercard will go up to $150 a year from $99. That is the first hike since 2018, when it raised the fee from $95 to $99, an airline spokeswoman said.
The Citi AAdvantage Business Mastercard will also have a fee increase and will now cost $150 a year.
Airlines and their bank partners have been steadily raising fees on rewards credit cards.
Those cards generate billions of dollars a year for airlines, which make money when miles are sold to banks, which then give them to customers. American's move, announced Tuesday, follows similar increases by rivals such as United Airlines .
Meanwhile, American Express last year raised the fee on its popular Platinum card , which comes with airport lounge access, to $895 a year from $695. JPMorgan Chase increased the annual fee on its competing card, the Sapphire Reserve , to $795 from $550.
The new perks for the American card include three times AAdvantage miles earnings on hotels booked through American's portal, a credit of up to $120 every four years for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck, and a $100 annual statement credit on in-flight purchases like food.
The new fees take effect Jan. 24.

articles.title_orig: 2026 Midterm Elections, Oct. 29
articles.title_zh: 2026 Midterm Elections, Oct. 29
articles.content_orig:
As the US midterm elections approach, we take a look at data to see a true picture of the US economy under Trump
With the midterm elections fast approaching, many Americans have the economy on their minds.
US voters are exhausted by years of higher prices. Donald Trump won the presidency in 2024 on promises to lower inflation and undo the damage he said the Biden administration had inflicted on the economy.
In Trump’s view, his plan is working. At a recent rally in Montana, Trump boasted about the current economy, framing it as a booming time for Americans. “We’re richer now,” he said. “We don’t have inflation.”
Economic data paints a different picture. Inflation , especially gas prices, has soared over the last year. The job market has been in stasis, and higher interest rates have meant it’s more expensive for Americans to borrow money for loans and mortgages.
These fluctuations have a concrete impact on the lives of Americans. A recent Harris poll for the Guardian found that a majority of Americans, including some Republicans, disagree. Nearly two-thirds said they believe the country is experiencing a recession, and many said higher prices had been a pain point. Americans are reporting having trouble saving, and a third polled said one surprise bill could sink them financially.
Here’s what the data shows us about Trump’s second term so far.
The rate of price increases has dramatically cooled since its peak in 2022, when the pandemic’s economic stimulus packages found their way into consumer prices. Inflation peaked at 9.1%, a 40-year high, in June 2022.
In January 2025, the month when Trump started his second term, inflation was down to 3%. By April 2025, it would be 2.3% – the lowest rate since 2021.
That’s when things start to get bumpy. After Trump placed tariffs on nearly everything that the US imports, inflation started to heat up again, climbing back up to 3% in September 2025. After many of his tariffs were paused and eventually found to be illegal, prices started going down again. In January and February 2026, inflation was back down to 2.4%.
The Iran war, specifically its impact on oil prices, has brought inflation back up to levels not seen since 2023. In May, inflation reached 4.2% and has hovered above 3.4% since.
It’s been nearly six years since Americans have seen inflation at a manageable 2% level. Price increases build up over time and can put a squeeze on budgets, which is why it’s such a sensitive point for voters during a crucial election.
In the Guardian’s recent poll with the Harris Poll, gas prices were the most common pain point for Americans, with 83% saying they are making a dent in their current finances.
Soon after the war in Iran began, the strait of Hormuz, a key route that a fifth of the world’s oil typically passes through, was blocked off. Its closure has pushed up prices all around the world. Though the US itself is a major oil producer, prices have still surged since the war. The average price of gas was $4.32 per gallon in mid-October, according to AAA, nearly $1.30 a gallon higher than a year ago.
Even for an oil-producing state like Texas, a gallon of gas is $3.81 compared with $2.64 a year ago. Meanwhile, drivers in California, a state that imports much of its gas from overseas, are paying $6.21 per gallon.
The labor market is another metric used to measure the health of the economy, and while the US job market has seen some growth since Trump took office again, figures have fluctuated over the last year. In 2025, altogether 181,000 new jobs were added to the economy, compared with 2.2m jobs in 2024.
Employers have been dealing with a mixed landscape for hiring: harsher immigration policies, uncertainty from tariffs and higher prices for supplies have all meant slow job growth. The unemployment rate has remained low, though, at just over 4%. Economists call this a “low-hire, low-fire” economy, in which employers are neither hiring nor dismissing workers.
Though many Americans report struggling in today’s economy, a small group have never been wealthier. The stock market has continued to soar since Trump took office, recovering from dips seen during his initial tariff announcement and the early days of the Iran war.
Economists largely see AI investment as the leading factor in the stock market’s acceleration. Tech companies are spending billions of dollars investing in datacenters and for chips that are needed to power AI.
While many Americans are invested in the stock market through their retirement and pension funds, this growth has really been a boon for the top 1% wealthiest Americans, who own nearly half of the stock market investments.
Economists say higher prices paired with an exuberant stock market have led to a K-shaped economy , where the wealthier have never felt richer while everyday Americans continue to deal with tightened budgets from high prices.
Interest rates are often not as noticeable to consumers as gas or grocery prices, which they come across every day. The impact that higher interest rates have on the economy takes longer to appear and runs deep. Interest rates shape how much Americans pay to borrow money – to run their businesses, pay off car loans and buy their homes.
For the Federal Reserve, shifting interest rates is the tool it uses to balance the economy. Raising rates can cool the economy, bringing prices down, though at the risk of hurting the job market. Lowering rates can stimulate the economy at the risk of leading to more inflation.
When Trump entered office in January 2025, the Fed was in the middle of a series of interest rate reductions. Officials said they were seeing inflation cooling and slower growth in the labor market. Interest rates were at a range of 4.25% to 4.5% – 1% lower than they were a year ago.
Uncertainty around Trump’s new tariffs would ultimately lead officials to pause the reduction, though the president was still demanding lower rates. As tariffs proved to have less of a long-term effect on prices, the Fed started lowering rates again in fall 2025.
For months, the Fed held off on changing rates as the economic impacts of the war of Iran bore out. But in September, the Fed hiked rates for the first time since 2023, by a quarter point. The Trump-appointed Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, said that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”.
Higher interest rates have already had an impact on mortgage rates, which had dipped down to below 6% (for a 30-year mortgage) for the first time since 2022, in February, but are now up past 7%.

articles.title_orig: EasySMX S10 Lite Review: A Switch 2 Fidget Toy With A Weird Removable Faceplate
articles.title_zh: EasySMX S10 Lite Review: A Switch 2 Fidget Toy With A Weird Removable Faceplate
articles.content_orig:
EasySMX is using Elizabeth Holmes levels of pedantry with this faceplate situation.
Of all the Switch 2 controllers I've reviewed in 2026, this is probably the most unexpected pick. EasySMX isn't as well-known as 8BitDo or Turtle Beach, and the S10 Lite is its most pared-down Switch 2 gamepad, regularly listed for $40. The price is exactly what intrigued me about the S10 Lite in the first place, considering most Switch 2 controllers cost around $70, and Nintendo's own Pro Controller is $90. A feature-rich gamepad that can potentially compete with 8BitDo's incredible, $30 Ultimate 2C ? I'm here for it.
And then just as swiftly, I'm gone. While the EasySMX S10 Lite has supremely tactile buttons, Hall effect sticks with a soft-hit feel, motion controls and strong haptics, it also has a semi-transparent, magnetically attached faceplate that's so wonky and cheap-feeling that it overshadows the controller's more attractive features. I'm someone who tends to enjoy oddball ideas in my gaming accessories and I can't fully make sense of the S10 Lite faceplate. The way that EasySMX has chosen to market this removable piece of plastic, using misleading verbiage around the availability of custom options, has only poured fuel on the confusion fire.
First, the basics and the good bits. The EasySMX S10 Lite is indeed light and compact, with a creamy plastic finish along the body and an anti-slip diamond texture on the backs of the grips. There are two buttons on the rear of the controller, mappable by pressing and holding a small nearby input marked M. I wish the rear buttons crept up the sides of the grips more, allowing my fingertips to more comfortably hit them, but they're certainly within reach and nice to have. The S10 Lite comes in two colors, ice blue or pastel pink, and while the pink is clearly the cuter option, they're both charming.
There are some fabulous modern features built into the S10 Lite, including precise, anti-drift Hall effect analog sticks that hit the sides of their enclosures silently and super softly. The sound and feel is comparable to Nintendo's proprietary soft-hit action on the Pro Controller, which is a notable feat. That said, the stick click on the S10 Lite is a little too stiff for my liking, and it does make an audible pop when pressed. I'm not personally complaining about the noise, which I find soothing on an ASMR level, but it's notable when the sticks themselves are so darn pillowy otherwise.
The face buttons are tactile microswitches with a wonderfully clicky sound and feel. However, they're also fairly rigid, especially compared with something like the springy mechanical buttons on Razer's Wolverine V3 Pro (my personal favorite gamepad, though it only supports PC and Xbox, and also costs an eye-watering $200. See? I told you the price point was appealing here). The haptics in the S10 Lite are nice and strong, with four intensity settings, and at most they make a slight whining sound rather than grinding.
The bumpers and wide-flared triggers stand out prominently from the chassis, and the triggers have a clicky microswitch action like the face buttons. While I do adore fidget-toy features in my controllers — and the S10 Lite definitely delivers on this point — in-game, I prefer a smooth and sensitive Hall effect pull in the triggers. It's a tradeoff between satisfying sounds and modern comfort that you'll have to consider for yourself.
I like that the home, GameChat and capture buttons are lined up at the bottom of the controller's face, separate from the plus and minus inputs in the center of the pad. This configuration should reduce the number of random, accidental screenshots that you end up taking while trying to quickly open the inventory in Resident Evil Requiem or peep the menu in Hello Kitty Island Adventure , for completely random example.
The S10 Lite has nine-axis motion controls and a Turbo function that allows you to set input macros to a simple button combo. It's also able to wake up the Switch 2 from afar, one of the raddest features a controller can have. The quick-start card that's included in the box is actually helpful in terms of connecting the gamepad to the console. And what's more, there's a built-in toggle on the backside of the pad that lets you swap between Switch and Switch 2 compatibility, or PC, Android and iOS play. In the box, you get the gamepad, a charging cable and the instruction card.
The gamepad, of course, includes the faceplate, attached with four visible, circular magnets and some tension. When I pulled my S10 Lite out of the box, the bottom ridge of the faceplate wasn't fully tucked into place, raised in a way that was mildly infuriating but not clearly unintentional. It wasn't until I was fidgeting with the controller, waiting for a game to download, that I realized I could pop in the transparent-blue plastic so it sat flat along the bottom. Even still, the left side of my faceplate refuses to depress as deeply as the right, so there's a sliver of icy plastic peering over one grip, catching my fingertips and compelling me to pick at it. I may be able to adjust this by tightening a tiny screw on that side, but all things considered, I'd rather not have to.
This leads us to the obvious question: Why have a removable faceplate in the first place? It would make sense if EasySMX had, say, a marketplace of cute alternatives that anyone could purchase and swap into their own pad, allowing the brand to jump on trends and collaborate with cool creators, naturally extending the money-making potential of the S10 Lite. That would make perfect sense. But that's not what EasySMX is doing.
The controller's product page provides just one sentence about faceplates, reading, "DIY Your Controller: express your personality with DIY Magnetic Faceplates & Stickers, allowing you to swap covers instantly to match your mood or your favorite game theme." Those first three letters are doing the heavy lifting, since EasySMX doesn't actually sell replacement or custom faceplates of any kind. The only way to guarantee you'll get one is to make it yourself, but even then, it appears that 3D files and high-quality images of the faceplates aren't publicly available . The company also doesn't sell stickers, an additional accessory it mentions without prompting.
With this context in mind, it's unclear what EasySMX means by DIY Your Controller , but it feels like a purposefully misleading, weaselly turn of phrase — like Elizabeth Holmes saying to Nathan Fielder, "You can see everything."
EasySMX does hold giveaways for customized faceplates on Reddit and Discord every now and then, it seems, but these are scattered. It's possible that the company is gathering data and ramping up to produce faceplates that players can buy, but right now, they're weirdly unattainable.
I really like tactile buttons, soft-hit sticks and the idea of modular art on my controller, but I really, really hate being lied to, and it kinda feels like that's what EasySMX is doing with the faceplate situation. The EasySMX S10 Lite is fine for kids (or adults) who love a good click and don't mind a messy faceplate, but otherwise, this thing is never beating the 8BitDo Ultimate 2C in terms of affordability and features.

articles.title_orig: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines says its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing
ULAANBAATAR, Mongolia -- The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines said Thursday its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing.
The restrictions have raised concerns over potential revenue losses and disruptions to Mongolia’s massive mineral sector.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC, which operates Oyu Tolgoi, one of the world’s largest copper mines, said the number of truck convoys transporting copper concentrate across the Chinese border has fallen from the usual 12 to 13 per day to just around four. The restrictions affect vehicles crossing at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port, which is adjacent to Mongolia’s Gashuunsukhait Border Port.
The export cuts amount to a decline of about $300 million compared to normal operating conditions and could reach $1.2 billion if restrictions continue through the end of the year, local media reported on Wednesday.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC did not confirm the reported losses in a statement to The Associated Press on Thursday.
Mongolia is a major supplier of coal and copper to China, the world’s largest consumer of both commodities.
Mongolian border officials said the slowdown was related to infrastructure and technology upgrades at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port.
Authorities in China’s Inner Mongolia region did not immediately answer questions from the AP.
In August, Chinese authorities introduced an in-vehicle facial recognition system for truck drivers crossing the border, and installation and maintenance work have affected border processing capacity, according to the Mongolian border authorities.
Mongolia’s government said the Chinese embassy in Ulaanbaatar informed it that the work, originally due to end by late September according to Mongolian news reports, may continue until the end of December.
Mongolian Finance Minister Mendsaikhan Zagdjav said some ministers were instructed during a Cabinet meeting to visit the border crossing and meet with Chinese authorities, according to local news reports.
All transport routes on the Mongolian side remain open and the government was not aware of any political reasons behind the restrictions, said the minister of Road and Transport, Delgersaikhan Borkhuu.
Mongolia’s copper sector has become an increasingly important contributor to national export revenues. During the first nine months of 2026, copper concentrate exports reportedly reached 2 million tons.
The border crossing restrictions have also affected Mongolia’s coal exports through Gashuunsukhait, with the number of vehicles crossing falling to just over 1,000 a day from 1,300 a day, border authorities said.
Mongolia has abundant mineral resources, including coal, copper, gold, uranium and fluorspar, and its economy relies heavily on mining, which accounts for roughly a quarter of its GDP. It is particularly sensitive to disruptions to cross-border trade and fluctuations in commodity prices.
Last year, coal and copper concentrates together accounted for 82.3% of Mongolia’s merchandise exports, while 89.4% of total exports went to China. Mongolia was also China’s leading supplier of imported coking coal, accounting for approximately 51% of Chinese coking coal imports in 2025.

articles.title_orig: Volkswagen ‘Must Act Quickly’ After Largest Loss in Over a Decade
articles.title_zh: Volkswagen ‘Must Act Quickly’ After Largest Loss in Over a Decade
articles.content_orig:
Deliveries in China fell more than 30% in the first nine months as the automaker pursues a restructuring that could cut up to 100,000 jobs
Volkswagen reported an after-tax loss of €5.8 billion ($6.5 billion) for the July-September quarter on Thursday as a write-down on its Porsche stake and falling sales in China weighed on results.
Revenue fell 6.3% from a year earlier. Earnings were dented by a charge of €6.4 billion that marked down what Volkswagen’s Porsche holding is worth. The operating loss grew to roughly €5.9 billion, compared with €1.3 billion a year earlier.
The quarterly loss was the biggest since 2015, the year a diesel emissions-cheating scandal engulfed the company, according to The New York Times . Deliveries in China were down by over 30% between January and September.
"We cannot afford to lose any time and must act quickly and decisively," Arno Antlitz, Volkswagen's chief financial officer, said in a statement.
Volkswagen said it expects 2026 Group sales revenue of around €315 billion and an operating return on sales of up to 1%. In the Automotive Division, it expects net cash flow of €3 billion to €6 billion and net liquidity of €32 billion to €34 billion.
The company said the forecast assumes the current tariff situation in international trade stays unchanged. It leaves out any effect from a Middle East escalation, from Group Target $TGT Picture 2030 and from the sale of a majority stake in Everllence.
Volkswagen in September cut its full-year profit outlook , citing about €10 billion in one-time charges concentrated at Porsche, along with U.S. tariffs and a weaker Chinese auto market. The new target of an operating return on sales of up to 1% replaced a range of 4% to 5.5%.
Antlitz said Volkswagen's electric models bring in smaller profits than its gasoline and diesel cars.
The supervisory board approved a restructuring plan in September that doubles planned job losses to 100,000 and halves the model lineup. The plan could also close four German plants, according to The Associated Press . Volkswagen is aiming to trim roughly €31 billion ($35 billion) from its expenses, according to The New York Times.

articles.title_orig: Greek container ship sinks after drone attack off Bulgaria
articles.title_zh: Greek container ship sinks after drone attack off Bulgaria
articles.content_orig:
By The Maritime Executive 2026-10-28 14:37:17
A Greek-owned containership operating a route for Zim was struck off Bulgaria midday on Wednesday, October 28, with the Bulgarian Navy rescuing the crew. The latest attack on commercial shipping in the western Black Sea came as the ministers from Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey were meeting to coordinate their security efforts.
The ministers issued a statement calling for “an immediate halt to attacks that threaten commercial vessels, maritime infrastructure, and the safety of maritime activities.” They said they believe the risks grow each day and said they were committed to working together to increase security.
Evidence of the increased risks was announced by the Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov, who reported that a rescue operation was underway in the Black Sea. He said that a French maritime patrol aircraft flying over the western part of the Black Sea had provided information to the Naval forces’ operation center. Reuters reported yesterday that France had relocated its Atlantique 2 maritime patrol aircraft to an air base in Romania as of October 18 and it would be conducting surveillance missions until November 6.
The Bulgarian Navy reports that the containership Contship Jet was struck by a surface drone at approximately noon while the vessel was 17 miles east of Cape Kaliakra near Varna. The Navy sent three vessels, along with one vessel from the Border Police. Reports say the 18,000 dwt containership was struck by three drones, which started a fire and left the vessel with a heavy list.
The Navy evacuated eight seafarers and located 10 others who were in the ship’s lifeboat. They were all in good condition and transferred to Varna. Four of the crewmembers are reported to be Ukrainians and 14 from the Philippines.
The Contship Jet was built in 2007 and has a capacity for 1,276 TEU. It is registered in Liberia and has been operating for Contships Management of Greece since 2019. It is listed as operating on the Levant – Black Sea Express route for ZIM and was coming from Ashdod and Haifa, Israel. It makes stops in Romania and Bulgaria before a stop in Egypt on the return voyage. It was reported to be carrying 421 containers.
Speaking to the media after the meeting in Sofia, Bulgaria, the ministers said, “To date, numerous commercial vessels have been attacked by the parties in the Black Sea, while drifting mines, unmanned surface vessels (USVs) and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that went out of control or were struck, as well as missile debris, have been destroyed.”
Reports indicate that the Contship Jet was the ninth vessel struck since the start of October in the western Black Sea. Reuters reports that a total of 34 sailors have been killed or are missing from these attacks.
Get the latest maritime news delivered to your inbox daily.
Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey agreed to a series of coordination steps, including strengthening intelligence sharing and improving early warning systems. Turkey’s National Defense Minister Yasar Guler said his country also reserves all its legal rights and might pursue legal action concerning the attacks on Turkish-flagged or operated vessels.
Bulgarian officials also said that they were monitoring the capsized vessel Khoryv (IMO 8138712) as it drifted into the country’s waters. The Comoros-flagged ship (3,280 dtw) was struck on October 23, killing one crewmember, leaving three missing, and nine rescued by the Romanians. Bulgaria warned the vessel was drifting into its zone, and its navy was planning to inspect the wreck. Today, the maritime authorities issued a warning to remain at least half a nautical mile from the ship, which is now 13 nautical miles east of Cape Sivri Burun in northernmost Bulgaria and drifting to the southwest. Bulgaria said it is prepared to act if the wreck continues to approach its shores.

articles.title_orig: ‘Catastrophic’: Medicare Part D changes could swallow your Social Security COLA raise
articles.title_zh: ‘Catastrophic’: Medicare Part D changes could swallow your Social Security COLA raise
articles.content_orig:
Social Security benefits are rising by 3.6% in 2027.
Even an increase that large might fall short in keeping up with inflation.
A new COLA formula could give Social Security recipients more buying power, but lawmakers may be hesitant to implement such a change.
The $23,760 Social Security bonus most retirees completely overlook ›
If you're on Social Security, you may be excited for January to arrive. At that point, benefits are expected to rise by 3.6% as the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment , or COLA, takes effect.
Given that 2026's Social Security COLA only came in at 2.8%, a 3.6% increase reads like a welcome change. But due to a flaw in the way Social Security COLAs are calculated, a 3.6% raise may not help you keep up with inflation in the new year after all.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
The purpose of Social Security COLAs is to help benefits keep up with inflation. There are many Social Security recipients who collect benefits for decades. Without an inflation adjustment, those checks would be guaranteed to lose purchasing power over time.
COLAs used to get voted in by lawmakers. Now, Social Security benefits are eligible for a COLA each year automatically.
When there's a year-over-year increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W, during the third quarter of the year, Social Security benefits increase as well. When there's a decrease or the CPI-W remains flat, Social Security benefits stay the same.
The problem is that the CPI-W does not accurately reflect the costs seniors on Social Security tend to face. Retirees on Social Security tend to spend their money very differently than wage earners, which makes the current formula less effective.
The Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group, says Social Security recipients have lost 13.7% of their buying power since 2016 due to insufficient COLAs. The group, along with other advocates, has pushed for a change to the COLA formula as a result.
Basing Social Security COLAs on the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly, for example, could help benefits better keep up with rising costs. That index would give categories like healthcare more representation, so that when Medicare and related costs rise, the increases are reflected in the COLAs Social Security benefits receive.
Unfortunately, there's been no indication that lawmakers are looking to change the Social Security COLA formula anytime soon. So seniors may have to grapple with somewhat ineffective raises for the foreseeable future.
If you're on Social Security, you may expect to be in a more comfortable financial position in 2027. But that may not happen.
It's important to realize that, even though Social Security's COLAs are meant to help benefits keep up with rising costs, they often fail to do so to some extent. Having a backup plan is therefore key. That plan could include reduced spending, part-time work, or another type of supplemental income.
If you're like most Americans, you're a few years (or more) behind on your retirement savings. But a handful of little-known "Social Security secrets" could help ensure a boost in your retirement income.

articles.title_orig: An AI Breakthrough Has Made Decades of Computer Science Research ‘Irrelevant’
articles.title_zh: An AI Breakthrough Has Made Decades of Computer Science Research ‘Irrelevant’
articles.content_orig:
Linköping University professor Peter Jonsson is set to have his work presented in two weeks’ time at one of the most prestigious conferences in theoretical computer science. As of Monday, much of that work is “dead,” he says, after AI showed that a 27-year-old hypothesis underpinning it is wrong.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic claimed this week to have disproved the exponential time hypothesis (ETH). Vast swaths of theoretical computer science research on complexity and algorithm design have been built on the premise that the effort it takes to solve certain problems increases exponentially with the size of the problem.
Jonsson expects his predicament will be “very common” at the IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, where his work will be presented by one of his coauthors. “People will start the talks: ‘ETH is false, half of my paper does not work,’” he says. It’s a vexing problem, Jonsson says, “but at the same time, we learn a lot from it. And this is what science is about.”
Researchers haven’t independently verified, let alone had time to fully understand, the AI-produced proofs, which both firms have published on GitHub in both natural language and its machine-checkable Lean format. OpenAI has asked the UC Santa Barbara computer scientists who originally proposed the hypothesis, plus an MIT academic who has refuted a version of ETH, to rally researchers to unpack the proofs. So far, this effort includes a Google form asking for volunteers and feedback, and a commitment from OpenAI to fund a conference on the topic.
UC Santa Barbara professor Daniel Lokshtanov plans to join the effort, as he estimates the result—if confirmed—will render him “galactically wrong” and make around 50 of his published papers either “pointless” or in need of a revisit.
“It’s just a giant bomb dropped into the middle of the field,” he says. “It’s really cool and terrible at the same time.”
Thore Husfeldt, head of the algorithms research group at the IT University of Copenhagen, had spent most of this year thinking about one single problem in his subfield. “As far as I can tell, it’s now all irrelevant,” he tells WIRED. Having first formulated a version of the hypothesis now disproved by OpenAI, he has been writing calculations on his blackboard to figure out what other parts of his work might have become obsolete due to the “once-in-a-generation result.” Unlike the ennui that has gripped math researchers who have faced similarly field-upending proofs generated by AI models, though, Husfeldt expressed enthusiasm about the new results.
The finding is “fantastic,” he says. “Being a mathematician is a lot like stumbling about in a completely dark room,” he explains. “It's like somebody just illuminated an entire subfield in floodlights of knowledge, and now we just run around like overexcited bunnies and look at all the nooks and crannies that we can suddenly explore. So it’s a super exciting time.”
For centuries, science has advanced through making hypotheses and proving them wrong. It also isn’t unusual for an academic to be scooped or have their work otherwise undercut by another research group. But AI has accelerated this, obliterating whole research programs and spooking researchers in specific fields of math and science who wonder where they stand now that machines can outperform them.
“The last few months have been really tough. It's a lot of doom and gloom, because every week, or every second week, the results announced by AI just annihilate the ongoing research projects of many people,” Husfeldt says. “That is psychologically taxing for many people,” he says, adding that his department has considered hiring an occupational psychologist because “some people are really depressed and really sad.”
Researchers have also been overwhelmed by the volume of content now being produced, thanks to AI, including slop-level results. Midway through the interview, Husfeldt receives what he suspects to be an AI-generated 17-page paper on the consequences of the ETH result from a random Gmail account. He won’t read it: “Reading math is a very big investment of cognitive time,” he says.
OpenAI has directly contributed to this; earlier this month, it dumped 722 manuscripts on 400 problems on GitHub, to the annoyance of academics , who complain this makes it difficult to digest the results. Adding to the frustration were several documents that contained errors, reflecting what some mathematicians saw as a hasty rollout designed to juice the company’s planned initial public offering rather than moving the field forward. This time around, OpenAI’s 60-odd-page paper on ETH seems to be written better than the companies’ past publications, academics tell WIRED.
They are now scrambling to unpack the paper and find what other results they can quickly deduce from it.
If ETH is false and it doesn’t, in fact, take exponentially more time to solve problems as they become more complex, that’s “exciting,” says Victor Lagerkvist, an associate professor at Linköping. He plans to return to problems he had previously given up on under the assumption ETH was accurate.
OpenAI’s finding could also have impacts on the cryptography that underpins web security, which is based on the assumption that certain mathematical problems take an impractically long time to solve. While this particular result doesn’t directly affect cryptography, “it should definitely scare some cryptosystem designers,” says Lokshtanov.
That’s why continued human and AI-assisted work in theoretical computer science is important, Husfeldt adds: “We want the open scientific process to identify our misunderstandings about computation, in particular because lots of modern digital infrastructure is built on assumptions about computation.”
As for Linköping’s Jonsson, he plans to revisit both his own and others’ papers that hinge on ETH being true, and believes his conference paper may eventually be salvageable through another method. He’s excited to look into the details of OpenAI’s proof and see what he can learn from it and apply it to new problems. Even though it undoes the assumptions underpinning his work, having a verdict for ETH is something he could only “dream of” before, he says. “These are exciting times,” he adds. “Most people would never experience anything like this in their career.”
“I don’t care if it's a human-written proof, or it's written by AI, or if an alien transmitted this proof to us. If it’s true, then we must simply use it in the future.’’

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Ship on fire in Strait of Hormuz as Hegseth fires top general accused of leaking war info
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Ship on fire in Strait of Hormuz as Hegseth fires top general accused of leaking war info
articles.content_orig:
Vice President JD Vance has sent a letter to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei seeking to restart peace negotiations, according to multiple reports, but President Trump insists it is a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Mr. Trump has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he is still mulling whether to resume major military operations against Iran or make a peace deal after next week's midterm elections, according to various outlets.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Vance was engaging directly with Mohsen Rezaei, one of Iran's most powerful hard-liners, in an effort to revive negotiations, citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter.
Vance sent the letter to Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' longest-serving former commander, at President Trump's direction, according to The Journal. The initiative seeks to establish whether Washington and Tehran can find common ground to avert a renewed conflict, the paper reported.
According to The New York Times , the letter, sent last week via Qatari mediators and delivered to Rezaei on Sunday, proposed an early meeting between American and Iranian officials, with Vance offering to lead the U.S. negotiating team.
The Times said Rezaei was expected to issue a formal response by Thursday. The letter did not specify a date or location for negotiations, but U.S. and Iranian officials were quoted by the newspaper as saying direct talks could begin as soon as next week in Qatar or Turkey.
According to Axios , Vance's letter explicitly stated that any negotiations aimed at preventing new U.S. military strikes would require discussions on Iran's nuclear program.
Asked Wednesday about Vance's contact with Iranian officials, Mr. Trump told reporters he had not sought to renew peace talks, but "what that is, they [Iran] need help with medical supplies and various things. He [Vance] asked me what I thought and I said, 'If you want to do that that's okay.' Basically it's getting supplies in to help people who are not well."
An official briefed on the diplomacy confirmed to CBS News Wednesday that Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war.
A response is expected from Tehran by the end of the week, most likely Saturday, the official added.
On Wednesday, a senior Iranian official denied Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal on Sunday, saying instead Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas , Reuters reported.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' said Thursday that three oil tankers exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines while attempting to transit what it described as "the unauthorized southern route" through the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy's public relations office said the incidents occurred over the past 24 hours, adding that the vessels were subsequently stranded along the southern shores of the strait.
The U.S. has encouraged shippers to use a southern shipping lane through the vital waterway, which President Trump himself declared mine-free at the end of August. Iran insists vessels can only transit the strait through routes it administers closer to its coast in the north of the strait, in coordination with Iranian authorities.
"These oil tankers had switched off all their radar and navigation systems," the IRGC added, referring to a common practice for vessels trying to avoid either U.S. or Iranian-imposed blockades in the strait and surrounding waters.
The vessels, "disregarding warnings from the IRGC Navy, were attempting to exit through the unauthorized southern route of the Strait of Hormuz when they struck naval mines and exploded," the IRGC said.
The IRGC said it held the vessels' owners and crews responsible for using the route that Tehran has warned against for months.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, a Pentagon official has told CBS News, after he was accused of leaking classified information related to the Iran war.
Sylvia was removed on Wednesday as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, becoming the latest in a series of generals to be ousted by Hegseth.
U.S. officials have told several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week's midterm elections – as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, two diplomats briefed on the matter told the Associated Press.
President Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, stressed. He has, however, repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections are over.
Those threats and the fresh U.S. urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation have put the region on alert for a possible return to major operations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month, which was summarily rejected by Mr. Trump, but which Iran still wants to see used as the basis for a new ceasefire agreement.
The U.S. has told regional allies that a new round of military action could last for just several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate, which could bring longer-term fighting, the diplomats told the AP.
The allies have also been urged by U.S. officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran's response would include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure.
The master of a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz reported seeing another vessel on fire nine nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, on Thursday, a monitoring agency run by the British military said.
The crew's status wasn't known and there was no damage assessment or report on the incident's environmental impact, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre added.
The strait is a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies. Since the start of the Middle East war in February, Iran has sought to control the waterway and has attacked ships it accuses of passing through the waterway without authorization.
The United States has responded with a counterblockade of Iranian ports.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the group at the kingdom's eastern region.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Eastern Province," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X.
Saudi Arabia has this month come under sustained attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport that was the kingdom's deadliest in years.
The Houthis said this week they had targeted the Ras Tanura refinery in the oil-rich Eastern Province with a ballistic missile.
Tehran has denied having anything to do with attacks by the Houthis after Saudi Arabia accused Iran of having encouraged the group's escalation against the kingdom.
Following an uneasy four-year truce, fighting reignited in Yemen in July, months into the U.S.-Iran conflict that has plunged the wider region into crisis.

With 85% of ballots counted, the right-wing bloc of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a slight lead over the main opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, but was still short of a majority after Tuesday's election.

articles.title_orig: Christine Lagarde to Step Down as Chief of European Central Bank
articles.title_zh: Christine Lagarde to Step Down as Chief of European Central Bank
articles.content_orig:
Departure of Lagarde, seen as candidate to take over World Economic Forum, comes as eurozone struggles with weak growth and inflation
Christine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, is stepping down nine months early, ending months of speculation about her future.
The European Central Bank (ECB) announced on Thursday morning that Lagarde would step down as its president on 7 February 2027; her term was scheduled to run until the end of October next year.
The ECB’s governing council thanked Lagarde warmly and gave her a longstanding ovation, as it met to set interest rates across the eurozone.
In a video message on social media, Lagarde said it had been a “great pride and huge privilege” to serve at the ECB.
“I think that I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future,” she added.
Lagarde has been seen as a candidate to take over the running of the World Economic Forum, which holds its annual meeting in Davos each January. The WEF founder, Klaus Schwab, stepped down last year after being accused of financial and ethical misconduct – which he denies.
Lagarde’s early departure fires the starting gun on the race to replace her as ECB chief, at a time when the eurozone is struggling with weak growth and above-target inflation. Potential candidates include the former Dutch central bank president Klaas Knot, the Spanish banker Pablo Hernández de Cos, the German central bank president, Joachim Nagel, and Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank.
The European Council appoints the head of the ECB, which sets monetary policy across the eurozone.
“The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that rightwing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April/May 2027,” said Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg bank.
“Lagarde’s successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Élysée Palace. He is a long-term political adversary of Le Pen.”
Lagarde joined the ECB in late 2019, shortly before the start of the Covid pandemic . During her tenure the ECB has also faced the economic consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war and the Middle East conflict and Donald Trump’s trade war.

The ECB is widely expected to keep interest rates on hold on Thursday afternoon.
Lagarde was wearing two plasters on her face in her video message, which she said was because of “a small surgery earlier in the week”.
She added: “Follow doctor’s orders and get your skin checked regularly.”

articles.title_orig: Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
articles.title_zh: Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
articles.content_orig:
Students gifted only water celery or white wormwood, choosing these fragrant plants to symbolise a pure pursuit of knowledge
While it is common for Chinese people to hold banquets for teachers upon graduation as a way of honouring them – a traditional value – in ancient China, students expressed their respect for teachers differently: by presenting them with vegetables.
The tradition began in the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC). On the first day of school, students wore blue gowns and brought their teachers wild vegetables they had gathered themselves. They then bowed reverently before memorial tablets honouring ancient sages. The ceremony was followed by a group dance, which also expressed the students’ respect for their teachers and their dedication to their studies.
Not just any vegetables could be presented to teachers on this day. Water celery and white wormwood were preferred because they were seen as clean, fragrant and ethereal, symbolising the students’ pure pursuit of knowledge.
